Sprang
SPRANG
v. (past t.)
The past tense of spring, Saxon springan, to leap, to shoot up. Webster 1828: leaped; shot up; issued or proceeded from. Scripture uses it of seed on stony ground, of seed on good ground, of a nation from one dead man, and of the Lord’s descent from Judah.

Biblical Definition

Sprang is used of sudden growth, and the parable of the sower turns on the fact that sudden growth is not by itself a good sign. And some fell on stony ground, where it had not much earth; and immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of earth (Mark 4:5) — and the speed is the symptom, not the promise; the shallow soil warms fastest and the plant that comes up quickest is the one that withers when the sun is up. The same verb describes the fourth soil, where the result is different: And other fell on good ground, and sprang up, and bare fruit an hundredfold (Luke 8:8). Hebrews uses it of a nation issuing from an old and childless couple: Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable (Hebrews 11:12). And it is used of the Lord’s tribal descent, in an argument about His priesthood: For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood (Hebrews 7:14) — He is a priest of another order entirely, after Melchisedec.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives SPRANG as the past tense of SPRING: leaped; bounded; shot up or forth, as a plant; issued or proceeded, as from a source or an ancestor.

expand to see more

SPRANG, pret. of SPRING — Leaped; bounded; darted or shot forward.

Shot up; grew; as a plant issuing from the ground.

Issued or proceeded, as from a source, a stock, or an ancestor; as, he sprang from an ancient family.

Arose or came into being; as, a thought sprang up in the mind.

From Saxon springan, to leap — the root also of spring the season, and spring a fountain.

Key Scripture

Mark 4:5 — "And some fell on stony ground, where it had not much earth; and immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of earth:"

Luke 8:8 — "And other fell on good ground, and sprang up, and bare fruit an hundredfold. And when he had said these things, he cried, He that hath ears to hear, let him hear."

Hebrews 11:12 — "Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable."

Hebrews 7:14 — "For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood."

Modern Corruption

Mark 4:5 makes rapid, joyful growth the mark of the stony-ground hearer rather than of the good-ground hearer, which is the reverse of the assumption on which most evangelistic follow-up operates.

expand to see more

The Lord’s own explanation is explicit: the stony-ground hearers when they have heard the word, immediately receive it with gladness; and have no root in themselves, and so endure but for a time: afterward, when affliction or persecution ariseth for the word’s sake, immediately they are offended. Two immediatelys frame the whole account — immediate reception and immediate offence — and the depth of the soil, not the speed of the shoot, decides everything. Modern evangelistic practice measures precisely the wrong variable: the immediate emotional response is counted, celebrated, and reported, while root is neither visible nor countable. Nothing here forbids joy at conversion; the good ground bears fruit too. It forbids treating the speed of the response as evidence of its reality.

Hebrews 7:14 uses the word in an argument of great weight for the doctrine of Christ’s priesthood. Our Lord sprang out of Judah, and Moses said nothing about priesthood for that tribe — the Levitical office belonged to Aaron’s line alone. Therefore His priesthood is not Aaronic but of another order, after Melchisedec, held not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life. That is why the Roman doctrine of a continuing sacrificing priesthood is an anachronism: the Levitical order has been superseded, and the one Priest who remains ever lives to make intercession. Hebrews 11:12 supplies the other note, and it is a mercy to anyone waiting: a nation as numerous as the stars sprang from one man who was as good as dead.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anatello (G393), to rise, to spring up; phuo (G5453), to grow, to spring up; exanatello (G1816), to spring up out of; Hebrew tsamach (H6779), to sprout, to spring forth.

expand to see more

Greek exanatello (G1816) — to spring up out of; the quick shoot on stony ground (Mark 4:5).

Greek phuo (G5453) — to grow, to spring up; sprang up, and bare fruit an hundredfold (Luke 8:8).

Greek anatello (G393) — to rise, to spring; our Lord sprang out of Juda (Hebrews 7:14), with the messianic overtone of a rising branch.

Hebrew tsamach (H6779) — to sprout; the root of tsemach, the Branch, a messianic title (Zechariah 3:8).

Greek rhiza (G4491) — a root; have no root in themselves (Mark 4:17).

Usage

"Immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of earth (Mark 4:5) — the speed is the symptom, not the promise."

"Sprang up, and bare fruit an hundredfold (Luke 8:8) — the same verb, and a different soil."

"Our Lord sprang out of Juda (Hebrews 7:14) — a priesthood of another order altogether."
